title: The Amazon Rainforest
summary: Why the Amazon Rainforest is the world's largest rainforest, the huge variety of life it holds, and why people call it the "lungs of the Earth."
poll: Protecting faraway forests like the Amazon is not something ordinary people can really affect.

versions.title: The Biggest Rainforest
versions.text:
The Amazon is a forest. It is very big. It is a rainforest. It is in South America.

Rain falls almost each day. It is warm. It is wet. The trees are tall. Their leaves are big and green. The ground is soft and dark.

Many animals live here. Monkeys jump in the trees. Birds fly above. Frogs and snakes hide on the ground. Bugs live here too.

We call this life biodiversity. It means many kinds of life in one place. This place has a lot of it.

Trees make fresh air for us. We call this air oxygen. We need it to breathe. It keeps us alive.

This place makes a lot of it. Some call it the lungs of the Earth. It helps the whole world.

versions.title: The Amazon Rainforest
versions.text:
The Amazon is a huge forest in South America. It is the biggest rainforest on Earth. It stretches across several lands, including Brazil and Peru.

Heavy rain falls almost every day of the year. The trees are tall, with big, green leaves that block the sun. Plants grow fast and very close together. The ground stays damp and dark. Moss grows on the old tree trunks.

Many kinds of animals live here. Monkeys swing through the trees. Colorful birds such as parrots fly above. Frogs, bugs, and snakes hide near the ground.

So many kinds of life live together in this forest. We call this biodiversity. The Amazon holds more of it than almost any other place on Earth.

Trees take in a gas called carbon dioxide. They give off fresh oxygen for us to breathe. People call the forest the lungs of the Earth.

The Amazon matters to people everywhere, not only in South America. It helps keep the air clean and the climate steady for all of us.

versions.title: The Amazon Rainforest
versions.text:
The Amazon covers about five and a half million square kilometers of South America. It is by far the largest rainforest on Earth. It stretches across nine countries, including Brazil, Peru, and Colombia.

The tallest trees form a thick roof of leaves. This roof is called the canopy. Smaller plants grow down below it in the shade. Heavy rain falls almost every day. The forest stays warm, wet, and green all year.

This forest holds an amazing number of species. About ten percent of all known species on Earth live here. These include monkeys, sloths, jaguars, birds, and fish. New kinds are still found each year.

We use the word biodiversity for this huge variety of life. Few places on Earth come close to this much biodiversity.

Trees take in a gas and give off fresh oxygen through photosynthesis. Because of this, people call the Amazon the lungs of the Earth.

The mighty Amazon River flows through the heart of this forest. It carries more water than any river on Earth, feeding the whole river basin.

The Amazon helps regulate rainfall and heat far beyond South America. That is why people study and work hard to protect it.

versions.title: The Amazon Rainforest: Lungs of the Earth
versions.text:
The Amazon covers roughly five and a half million square kilometers of South America. It is by far the largest rainforest on Earth. It stretches across nine countries, including Brazil, Peru, and Colombia. It holds about a third of all the tropical rainforest left on the whole wide planet today.

The tallest trees form a dense canopy of leaves high above. Smaller plants crowd into the shadowy understory beneath, competing for scraps of sunlight that filter down. Heavy rain falls almost every single day of the year. This keeps the ecosystem warm, humid, and green through every single season.

This single ecosystem sustains an extraordinary number of species. Scientists estimate that roughly ten percent of all known species on Earth live within it. These include monkeys, sloths, jaguars, and countless birds, fish, and insects found nowhere else in the world. New species are still discovered every single year, even now.

Through photosynthesis, the forest's billions of trees absorb carbon dioxide and release fresh oxygen. Much of this oxygen is reused by the forest's own decomposing plants and animals, rather than escaping outward into the wider atmosphere beyond.

The mighty Amazon River winds through the heart of this rainforest. It carries more water than any other river on Earth, draining an immense basin larger than most countries. This drainage system sustains the forest's remarkable growth across the whole region.

Indigenous communities have inhabited the Amazon for thousands of years. They developed deep knowledge of its plants and rivers long before any outside expedition ever arrived to study them. Twentieth-century expeditions began documenting the forest's species in a more formal, scientific way.

The Amazon regulates rainfall and temperature far beyond South America. That is why protecting this ecosystem concerns scientists everywhere, not only the nine countries that contain it today.

versions.title: The Amazon Rainforest: Lungs of the Earth
versions.text:
Covering roughly five and a half million square kilometers of South America, the Amazon Rainforest ranks as by far the largest rainforest on Earth, a scale so vast that it defies easy comparison with any other ecosystem on the planet. It stretches across nine countries, including Brazil, Peru, and Colombia, and holds approximately a third of all remaining tropical rainforest found anywhere in the world.

The Amazon's towering trees form several distinct vertical layers, with the tallest specimens reaching far above the rest to create a dense roof of leaves known as the canopy, while smaller plants crowd together in the shadowy understory beneath it, competing fiercely for the scarce scraps of sunlight that manage to filter downward through countless layers of overlapping foliage. Heavy rain falls almost every day of the year, ensuring that the region remains warm, humid, and deeply green throughout every season without exception.

This single, continuous forest sustains an extraordinary range of vegetation and animal life unmatched almost anywhere else. Scientists estimate that the Amazon contains roughly ten percent of all known species on Earth, including thousands of kinds of birds, fish, insects, and mammals such as monkeys, sloths, and jaguars, a considerable number of which exist nowhere else in the world and remain vulnerable to even modest habitat loss.

Scientists use the term biodiversity to describe this enormous variety of organisms coexisting within a single region, and few places on the planet approach the Amazon's extraordinary biodiversity; new species continue to be discovered there every year, even now, as researchers push further into remote, previously unstudied stretches of the forest.

Through the process of photosynthesis, the Amazon's billions of trees absorb vast quantities of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and release fresh oxygen in return, and because of this continual exchange, people often call the Amazon the lungs of the Earth, though scientists are careful to note that much of this oxygen is ultimately reused by the forest's own decomposing organisms rather than escaping outward into the wider atmosphere.

The mighty Amazon River winds through the heart of this rainforest, carrying more water than any other river on Earth and sustaining the forest's astonishing growth across its immense drainage basin, a watershed larger than most entire continents.

Indigenous communities have inhabited the Amazon for thousands of years, developing profound, intricate knowledge of its plants, animals, and rivers long before any outside expedition ever arrived; in the twentieth century, scientific expeditions began systematically documenting the forest's species, though researchers still estimate that countless plants and insects there remain entirely unidentified, hidden within one of the most complex ecosystems humans have ever attempted to study.

The Amazon matters to the entire planet, not merely to the countries that contain it, because it helps regulate rainfall patterns and temperature across much of the globe, a fact that explains why protecting it from clearing and fire concerns scientists and governments on every continent.

MID.prompt: Explain why the Amazon Rainforest matters to the whole planet, not just to the countries where it is located. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained why the Amazon matters globally.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The Amazon Rainforest matters to the whole planet for several reasons. Through photosynthesis, its billions of trees absorb huge amounts of carbon dioxide and release fresh oxygen, which is why people call it the lungs of the Earth. The Amazon also helps regulate rainfall and temperature far beyond South America, affecting climate patterns across much of the globe. Because of these effects, protecting the Amazon from clearing and fire concerns scientists everywhere, not only the nine countries that contain it.

keyWords.example: Removing one species can disturb an entire ecosystem.

keyWords.example: Fungi grew quickly on the decomposing log.

keyWords.definition: originally living in a place, rather than arriving from somewhere else
keyWords.example: The exhibit featured tools made by an indigenous community long ago.

keyWords.definition: a long, organized journey made for a special purpose, such as exploring
keyWords.example: The scientists spent a year preparing for their expedition into the forest.

keyWords.definition: the way water flows off or through an area of land into rivers

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The Amazon Rainforest is an unmatched reservoir of global biodiversity whose scale and processes influence climate conditions well beyond South America.
The Amazon Rainforest has already had every one of its species fully identified and documented by scientists from around the world.
The Amazon River is more significant to the planet than the forest ecosystem surrounding it, since rivers hold more life than trees do.
The Amazon Rainforest's climate has remained completely unaffected by human activity, and it will stay the same in every future century, according to all of the scientists.
questions.why: The article explains the Amazon's scale, its extraordinary biodiversity, its photosynthesis-driven oxygen cycle, and its influence on global rainfall and temperature.

wrong.B: The article says countless plants and insects remain entirely unidentified.
wrong.C: The article presents the river as part of the larger rainforest ecosystem, not superior to it.
wrong.D: The article discusses clearing and fire as ongoing concerns, implying real impact from human activity.

questions.stem: Why do scientists describe the Amazon's biodiversity as especially vulnerable?
options: Every species in the Amazon can easily survive outside the forest
Every species in the Amazon can easily survive outside the forest without any special help or protection of any kind whatsoever
A considerable number of its species exist nowhere else and remain vulnerable to even modest habitat loss
The forest has already lost all of its original biodiversity
questions.why: The article explains that many Amazon species exist nowhere else in the world, making them especially vulnerable to habitat loss.

wrong.A: The article implies the opposite: many species exist only in the Amazon and depend on it.
wrong.B: The article implies the opposite: many species exist only in the Amazon and depend on it.
wrong.D: The article describes thriving, extraordinary biodiversity, not a loss.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to much of the oxygen the Amazon's trees release through photosynthesis?
options: It immediately travels to every other continent on Earth
It is stored permanently inside the Amazon River
It converts back into carbon dioxide almost instantly as soon as it is released by the trees into the surrounding atmosphere
It is ultimately reused by the forest's own decomposing organisms rather than escaping into the wider atmosphere
questions.why: The article notes that scientists observe much of the forest's oxygen gets reused by decomposing organisms within the ecosystem rather than escaping outward.

wrong.A: The article does not describe oxygen traveling instantly across continents.
wrong.B: Rivers do not store oxygen in this way.
wrong.C: The article does not describe oxygen converting back into carbon dioxide instantly.

questions.stem: In the article, the word indigenous describes —
options: scientists who recently launched expeditions into the forest
communities that have inhabited a region for a very long time
animals found only in zoos outside South America
trees planted by modern conservation programs
questions.why: The article describes indigenous communities that have inhabited the Amazon for thousands of years, long before any outside expedition arrived.

wrong.A: Expedition scientists arrived much later, which is the opposite of indigenous.
wrong.C: The word does not describe zoo animals.
wrong.D: The word describes people, not planted trees.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why do researchers believe countless Amazon species remain unidentified?
options: The forest is one of the most complex ecosystems humans have ever attempted to study, with vast, remote areas still unexplored
No scientific expeditions have ever entered the Amazon, since the river is too dangerous for boats and for planes, and so the forest has never been studied by anyone, ever
All Amazon species were identified by indigenous communities centuries ago, and written down in books, so scientists believe that nothing is left to find in the forest
The forest is too small for many species to exist, so most animals have already left for other places, and researchers think few kinds of life remain in the Amazon today
questions.why: The article describes the Amazon as one of the most complex ecosystems ever studied, implying many remote areas and species remain unexamined.

wrong.B: The article describes twentieth-century scientific expeditions that did enter the forest.
wrong.C: The article does not claim indigenous communities identified every species in a formal scientific sense.
wrong.D: The Amazon is described as enormous, not small.

questions.stem: In what order did these developments most likely occur?
options: Twentieth-century expeditions document species, indigenous communities develop forest knowledge, the Amazon forms its current size
Indigenous communities develop forest knowledge, twentieth-century expeditions document species, researchers continue discovering new species today
Researchers continue discovering new species today, indigenous communities develop forest knowledge, twentieth-century expeditions document species
Twentieth-century expeditions document species, researchers continue discovering new species today, indigenous communities develop forest knowledge
questions.why: Indigenous communities developed deep forest knowledge over thousands of years first, twentieth-century expeditions then began documenting species, and new discoveries continue in the present day.

wrong.A: Indigenous knowledge developed long before any twentieth-century expedition.
wrong.C: Ongoing present-day discovery comes after, not before, the earlier developments.
wrong.D: Indigenous knowledge came first, before any expedition or present-day discovery.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the fact that the Amazon helps regulate rainfall and temperature far beyond South America?
options: Events and changes within the Amazon can affect climate conditions in distant parts of the world
The Amazon has no measurable effect outside its own basin, so far-off places need not worry
Only countries bordering the Amazon experience any climate effects from it, and no others
The Amazon's climate influence is purely a local legend told by villagers, with no scientific basis
questions.why: If the Amazon regulates rainfall and temperature well beyond South America, then changes inside the forest can influence climate conditions in distant regions.

wrong.B: The article states the opposite: its influence reaches far beyond its own basin.
wrong.C: The article says the effects reach the whole globe, not only bordering countries.
wrong.D: The article presents this as a scientific concern, not a legend.

questions.stem: Why does the author likely mention the Amazon's drainage basin near the discussion of the river?
options: To help readers imagine the immense scale of land that feeds and depends on the river system
To argue that the river should be renamed after the people who first lived nearby
To explain exactly how canoes are built by the people who live beside the river
To describe the diet of Amazonian fish in great detail, from the smallest to the largest ones
questions.why: Describing the drainage basin as larger than most continents helps readers grasp the enormous scale of land connected to the Amazon's river system.

wrong.B: The article does not discuss renaming the river.
wrong.C: The article does not explain canoe construction.
wrong.D: The article does not detail fish diets.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says protecting faraway forests like the Amazon is not something ordinary people can really affect. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the article about the forest's biodiversity, its global role, and its ongoing study.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that protecting faraway forests like the Amazon is beyond the reach of ordinary people. The article explains that the Amazon helps regulate rainfall and temperature across much of the globe, which means its health affects everyone, not only the nine countries that contain it. The forest's extraordinary biodiversity, including species found nowhere else, depends on choices made far from the Amazon itself, such as what products people buy and support. Someone might argue that one person cannot influence a forest thousands of kilometers away, but widespread public attention and support for conservation efforts have measurably slowed clearing and fire in protected areas, showing that distant concern can still make a real difference.
